title: The Elements
tagline: Thirteen books that defined the shape of reason forever.

scenes.text: Alexandria, 300 BCE. The greatest library the world has ever seen. Euclid of Alexandria is writing — not just recording what he knows, but building a logical architecture that will hold for two thousand years: thirteen books proving everything in geometry from five simple assumptions.

scenes.speaker: Euclid
scenes.text: A point has no part. A line has breadth-less length. Begin there. Everything else follows.

challenge.question: Euclid worked in which great ancient city?
challenge.fact: Euclid worked at the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy I around 300 BCE. When Ptolemy asked if there was a shorter way to learn geometry, Euclid reportedly replied: 'There is no royal road to geometry.'

scenes.text: Euclid's proof that prime numbers are infinite is one of the first genuine proofs in mathematics — a demonstration so elegant it appears unchanged in textbooks today. His method: assume finitely many primes, multiply them together and add one, then show the contradiction.

scenes.speaker: King Ptolemy
scenes.text: Euclid. Is there not a shortcut to geometry?

challenge.fact: Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE) comprises 13 books and 465 propositions. It was used in university geometry courses until the early 20th century — over 2,000 years of continuous use.

Euclid classified all geometric knowledge. Test your knowledge with this classification crossword.
challenge.fact: Euclid's proof of the Pythagorean theorem occupies a full page of the Elements and uses nothing but logic. It remains one of the most beautiful proofs in all of mathematics.

scenes.text: Eratosthenes, who would later calculate the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy, studied in the same tradition as Euclid. Each generation of Alexandrian scholars built on the previous — standing, as Newton would say two thousand years later, on the shoulders of giants.

challenge.instruction: Prove Euclid's law of reflection — redirect the light beam to hit the target using mirrors.
challenge.fact: Euclid wrote 'Optica', one of the earliest works on optics and perspective, laying the groundwork for understanding how light behaves.

challenge.instruction: Euclid knew light reflects — but what about refraction? Route the beam through two fixed deflectors using two mirrors of your own.
challenge.fact: Euclid's 'Catoptrics' studied mirrors and reflection. It took nearly two thousand more years for Newton to explain why white light splits into a spectrum — but the geometry Euclid laid down made that discovery possible.
